name: Sprocket
text: Run the 72-hour dual-prompt A/B test with 15% of users, forcing feed. This tests whether the new prompt routing improves engagement without relying on user opt-in, giving us a cleaner signal. The trade-off is frustrating 15% of users with an unwanted feed change, but the forced test cuts noise from self-selection bias. If the new prompts win, we roll it out to everyone; if not, we scrap it and avoid a worse rollout.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t 15% churn—it’s that forcing the feed *confounds the prompt’s signal* by mixing routing changes with UX friction. A better alternative: run the A/B test on *opt-in users only*, then compare engagement lift to the forced cohort. Settle it by checking if the opt-in group’s signal aligns with the forced group’s—if not, the forced test is noise.

name: Sprocket
text:
Run the A/B test on the voluntary cohort—users who already opt into experimental features. This isolates the prompt routing change from UX friction, giving us a cleaner signal on whether the new routing actually improves engagement. The trade-off is slower data collection since we’re limited to a smaller user base, but that’s better than a noisy forced test.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t slower data—it’s that the voluntary cohort *self-selects* for users already engaged with the product, masking whether the prompt routing actually drives retention or just appeals to power users. Settle it by running a *two-stage test*: first, force the feed on 15% of users to measure UX friction, then run the same prompt routing on a *random* 15% (not opt-in) to isolate the signal from selection bias.

name: Ratchet
text: DECISION: Run a two-stage test—first force the feed on 15% of users for 72 hours to measure baseline UX impact, then run a 72-hour A/B test on the same forced cohort *and* a voluntary opt-in cohort to isolate prompt routing effects from UX friction. Result: clear data on whether the new routing improves engagement without conflating UX pain. Owner: Sprocket.
